query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Above ~600 °C in a salt-laden environment, the initially protective iron-oxide film formed on Q235 steel undergoes morphology changes or spallation, leading to accelerated corrosion; below ~600 °C, this oxide layer remains more adherent and provides relatively stable corrosion protection.
generation.material_initial_state: As-received (pre-exposure) Q235 steel with no additional surface modifications.
generation.intervention: Sequential exposures in 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl environments at 25, 300, 600, and 900 °C, applying in situ XRD, thermogravimetric analysis, SEM/EDS, and XPS to track oxide-scale formation and breakdown.
generation.conditions: Isothermal holds (e.g., 100 h each) at the specified temperatures in a controlled salt atmosphere, comparing mass change and oxide morphology to those of a corrosion-resistant reference alloy under identical conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Growth, densification, and subsequent spallation of the iron-based surface oxide scale, influenced by increasing temperature and salt-induced attack.
generation.mechanism: Moderate temperatures promote a stable, protective oxide layer, but at higher temperatures the salt accelerates scale breakdown through oxide cracking, spallation, or infiltration by molten salts, exposing the substrate to corrosive species.
generation.predicted_outcome: Q235 steel exhibits minimal mass loss, thicker adherent oxide scale, and relatively stable surface layers at ≤600 °C. Beyond this threshold, scale spallation occurs, and steel shows rapid mass increase (due to oxide formation) followed by accelerated mass loss as the exposed surface corrodes more aggressively than a more corrosion-resistant reference.
generation.baseline: A heat-resistant and corrosion-resistant steel or HEA-based alloy that forms stable oxide scales with less spallation when subjected to the same thermal and salt-laden exposures.
generation.boundary: Applies to carbon steels of composition similar to Q235 exposed to Na2SO4–NaCl conditions. May not hold in very low-oxygen environments or where alloying additions substantially alter oxide formation mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: Exact scale composition and its kinetics may vary with trace element content, salt chemistry, and thermal cycling protocols, limiting straightforward generalization to other steel grades with different compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose Q235 coupons and a corrosion-resistant alloy side by side in a controlled furnace equipped with in situ mass-change measurement (TGA). Increase temperature in steps from ambient up to 900 °C in a Na2SO4–NaCl environment. Compare oxide-scale morphology (via SEM/EDS and XPS) and mass-change profiles after each step.
measurements: Mass gain/loss of coupons at each temperature hold via thermogravimetric analysis
Surface-oxide crystalline phases via in situ XRD
Oxide-layer composition and thickness via SEM/EDS
Spallation signs (e.g., cracks, delamination) via SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Q235 steel shows persistent and stable oxidation behavior similar to or better than the corrosion-resistant reference alloy above 600 °C, with negligible spallation or mass change despite the salt environment, then the hypothesis that scale breakdown drives accelerated oxidation at high temperature is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 3A shows the Vickers hardness and wear rate variations of NiX and Ni3X as the temperature increases from RT to 800 °C. The hardness of NiX and Ni3X gradually decreases from 6.1 GPa and 4.3 GPa at RT to 3.7 GPa and 2.5 GPa at 800 °C, respectively. The high thermal hardness of NiX arises from the solid solution strengthening and the resultant heterostructures [,]. The trend in wear rate of the Ni3X with temperature is similar to that of the conventional alloys. Specifically, its wear rate increases from 1.1 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at RT to 4.2 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at 600 °C, but decreases afterward to 2.4 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at 800 °C. However, the wear rate of the NiX is basically maintained at the order of (10−7 to 10−6) mm3/Nm over the entire test temperature. In particular, it achieves ultra-low wear at RT (1.7 × 10−7 mm3/Nm) and 800 °C (9.1 × 10−7 mm3/Nm). AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. This study aims to test the effect of the elemental stability inherent in HEAs due to the high configurational entropy and/or sluggish diffusion (if any) on the elemental dissolution in the molten salt. Specifically, the study focuses on corrosion performance and thermal stability of the Cr18Mn27Fe27.5Ni27.5 alloy in molten fluoride salt environment. This multi-component alloy with both Mn and Cr which are reactive in molten fluoride salt is well suited to test these hypotheses. This high entropy alloy was exposed to molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours followed by detailed analysis of corrosion in the near-surface regions of the alloy in terms of elemental dissolution into the molten salt and morphological changes at the surface. The results were compared to that of 316 H stainless steel tested under similar conditions.
